title: Conduction and Fourier's law: heat flowing through a solid wall
examples: What is Fourier's law of conduction?
How do I calculate heat loss through a wall?

explain.say: Hold a metal spoon in hot tea and soon the handle is warm. Heat crawls through the solid from atom to atom, without the metal moving. That is conduction. Look at the wall: a warm room on one side, winter on the other, and heat flowing through the brick.

explain.say: In 1822 Joseph Fourier wrote the rule. The heat flow Q equals k, the thermal conductivity, times area times the temperature difference, divided by the thickness. Thicker walls and lower k let less heat through. Brick has k about 0.72 watts per metre kelvin. What do you think copper's k is?

explain.say: About 400, more than five hundred times brick! Now the numbers: 10 square metres of 200 millimetre brick, 20 degrees inside and 0 outside. Q is 0.72 times 10 times 20 over 0.2, which is 720 watts, like running seven 100 watt bulbs all day.

explain.say: Inside the wall the temperature falls in a straight line from 20 to 0. See the graph? Halfway through it is 10 degrees. The slope of that line is the temperature gradient, here 100 degrees per metre. Fourier says the heat flux is k times that gradient. What would a steeper line mean?

explain.say: More heat flowing! Well done. Real link: metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature because its high k pulls heat from your hand faster. Exam tip: keep L in metres and remember that a straight-line profile only holds for steady flow through a flat wall of one material.

faq.q: What is Fourier's law of conduction?
faq.a: Heat flux by conduction equals minus k times the temperature gradient. For a flat wall that gives Q equals k A delta T over L.

faq.q: How do I calculate heat loss through a wall?
faq.a: Multiply the thermal conductivity by the area and the temperature difference, then divide by the thickness. For 10 square metres of 200 millimetre brick with a 20 degree difference, that is 720 watts.
asks: heat loss through a wall formula

faq.q: What does the temperature profile in a wall look like?
faq.a: For steady conduction through one flat material it is a straight line from the hot face to the cold face. Its slope is the temperature gradient.
Thermal conductivity k measures how easily a material conducts heat, in watts per metre kelvin. Copper is about 400, brick about 0.7, mineral wool about 0.04.

faq.q: Why does metal feel colder than wood?
faq.a: Both are at room temperature, but metal conducts heat away from your skin much faster, so your skin cools and the metal feels cold.

facts: Joseph Fourier published The Analytical Theory of Heat in 1822.
Copper conducts heat about 10 000 times better than mineral wool insulation.

quiz.say: A glass window, 1.5 square metres and 5 millimetres thick, has k equal to 1 watt per metre kelvin. Its faces are at 15 and 5 degrees. What is the heat flow?
quiz.show: Glass: A = 1.5 m², L = 5 mm, k = 1 W/m·K, faces at 15 °C and 5 °C. Heat flow?
quiz.why: Q = 1 × 1.5 × 10 / 0.005 = 3000 W. (Real windows lose less, because air films add resistance.)

wrong.1: That uses 5 instead of 0.005 metres for the thickness.
wrong.2: A factor of ten slipped; 5 mm is 0.005 m.

quiz.say: You double the thickness of a wall and keep everything else the same. What happens to the conduction heat flow?
quiz.show: Double the wall thickness. Conduction heat flow becomes…
quiz.why: Q is inversely proportional to the thickness L.

wrong.1: Thicker walls let less heat through, not more.
wrong.2: Q goes as 1 over L, not 1 over L squared.
